questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [mid] an audit trail that is complete, queryable and does not leak (organized-experiment-internal-case-management-system, docs/learning/flow-traces.md). Scenario: an internal investigations desk with 12 teams and 300 staff makes about 20,000 case changes a day; compliance must be able to answer 'who changed case X, from what to what, and why' for 7 years; escalation reasons are confidential and only team leads, managers and auditors may read them; an automated overdue-deadline sweep also changes case status; staff leave and their accounts are deleted. Write your design before you look: which transaction an audit row is written in, which change paths must produce a row (human and automated), what a row records so that before and after are both visible, what a row must still say after its actor or case is deleted, how per-case and per-person questions are queried, who may read audit entries and through which endpoint, and how confidential text is kept out of audit payloads. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] Write the audit row inside the business write's transaction: the helper takes the caller's transaction client, so a rolled-back change leaves no audit row and a committed change cannot exist without one. Logging after the commit would leave history that is missing or misleading on rollback.

[w3] Every path that changes state must produce the same kind of row, the automated ones included: the overdue sweep moves cases to ESCALATED but records only that an escalation was auto-created, so the status change itself is missing from the trail. Route every status write through one function that also writes the transition row.
keyPoints.quote: (no `case.transitioned` row is written for the status change)

keyPoints.text: [w3] Record before and after for each changed field, not the request: the update path stores the raw request input as metadata, which shows only the values asked for and nothing about the values replaced, and copies whatever the client sent. Build metadata per action from an allow-list of fields with their old and new values.
keyPoints.quote: audit `case.updated` with the raw input as metadata

keyPoints.text: [w3] Keep confidential text in exactly one place: when an escalation carries a reason, store it as the restricted note and let the audit row point to that note by id, instead of copying the text into metadata where a second set of read rules would have to protect it.

[w2] Give audit reads their own rule and endpoint: today the case detail include returns the newest 20 audit rows, with the actor's name and email and the whole metadata, to anyone allowed to load the case, so case visibility silently becomes audit visibility. An audit-read permission with a paged, filterable endpoint serves compliance without widening what case workers see.

[w2] Make rows outlive their subjects: case and actor links are nullable with ON DELETE SET NULL, so the row survives a deletion but loses who acted. Store a snapshot of the actor (name, role, team) and the case number on the row at write time.

[w2] Index for the questions compliance asks: the only audit index is (case, created at), which serves a case timeline; 'what did this person do last quarter' needs (actor, created at), and 7 years at about 20,000 changes a day (roughly 50 million rows) calls for time partitioning so retention can drop whole partitions.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — the same desk six months later: a case worker opening the browser's network tab reads an escalation reason only leads should see; an auditor asks why a case closed on Tuesday shows ESCALATED on Wednesday and cannot find its history past the first screen; two leads change the same RESOLVED case at the same moment; and a departed employee's account is deleted. What breaks, how would you notice, and what is the repair?

keyPoints.text: [w3] The confidential reason is stored twice on an escalation, as a restricted note and as the comment field of the transition's audit metadata, while the detail serializer filters only the notes list and passes every other child through. So the API hands the reason to every role that can open the case. Repair: drop the text from metadata (point to the note) and run the audit rows through the same visibility rule as notes.

[w3] You would not notice it in the product, because the trail view renders only the action, the time and the actor; the leak exists only in the JSON. Protection that lives in the UI is not protection, so add an API-level test that loads a case as a role without restricted-note access and asserts the restricted text appears nowhere in the response.

[w3] The Tuesday-close mystery is the sweep: it compares against the status it read before its loop, moves the case to ESCALATED without the workflow check, and its audit row carries only the deadline id, so the trail shows no from/to for the jump and a just-closed case is silently reopened. Make the sweep's status change a conditional update that writes a real transition row.

[w2] The trail stops at 20 entries on the case page and there is no other read path for audit rows, so a long-lived case's older history is unreachable without database access. A paged audit endpoint ordered by time fixes the auditor's question.

[w2] Two concurrent changes from RESOLVED both pass validation, because the status is checked against the row read before the transaction and the update matches the case id only; the last commit wins and both audit rows claim to start from RESOLVED, so the trail records a transition that never happened as written. Put the expected current status in the update's WHERE and treat zero rows as a conflict.

[w2] Once the departed employee's user row is deleted, the rows they wrote no longer resolve to an actor, and the trail view labels any row without an actor 'System', so the history now credits an automated actor with a person's decisions. Snapshot the actor at write time and never render a missing actor as the system.

[w1] Fixing the code does not remove what already leaked: existing transition rows still hold confidential reasons in their metadata. Plan a one-off redaction of those rows, run as a privileged operation that is itself recorded, and tell compliance which rows were changed and why.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your audit design against the alternatives: writing audit rows in the business transaction versus shipping events to a separate log pipeline, free-form JSON metadata versus a declared shape per action, copying values into the row versus referencing them, returning the trail inside the case detail versus a separate audit endpoint, application-written rows versus database triggers, an ordinary table versus an append-only or tamper-evident store, and recording reads of confidential data or not. For each, say what you bought, what it cost, and which requirement put you on that side.

keyPoints.text: [w3] The same-transaction write is atomic and needs no new infrastructure, at the cost of a row on every business write in the main database and audit storage that grows with it. A separate log pipeline scales and isolates the trail but can lose or reorder entries unless the event itself is committed with the change; the 'complete' requirement keeps the write in the transaction.
keyPoints.quote: then one transaction (`:147-193`) that generates the case number (`:149`), inserts with `connect` relations (`:150-178`) and writes the audit row (`:180-190`)

keyPoints.text: [w3] Free-form metadata needs no migration per action, but nothing stops a call site from putting confidential text or a whole request body into it; a declared shape per action (an allow-list of fields) costs a schema change per new action and buys a reviewable contract for what the trail may contain.

[w3] Copying a value into the row makes the entry self-contained and immune to later edits, but every copy of confidential text is another place its read rule must be enforced; referencing the restricted note keeps one copy under one rule, at the cost of an extra lookup when an auditor needs the text.

[w2] Returning the trail inside the case detail costs one query and no extra endpoint, but makes audit visibility equal case visibility and caps history at the newest rows; a separate endpoint costs a permission, paging and an extra UI call, and buys a read rule of its own.

[w2] Rows written by the application know the actor and the intent (the reason, the action name); database triggers would also catch writes the application forgot, such as the sweep's status change or manual SQL, but they know nothing about the acting user unless it is passed down as a session variable. Pick application writes plus a test that every status writer emits a row, or add a trigger as a backstop.

[w2] The repository only ever creates audit rows, but the table itself is ordinary and the application's database role can update or delete it. Denying UPDATE and DELETE to that role, or chaining a hash through the rows, buys tamper evidence; it costs operational work and complicates a legally required erasure, which then needs its own recorded procedure.

[w1] Recording who read a confidential case answers 'who saw this reason', which a desk handling investigations may be asked; it costs a write on a read path and a much larger trail. Today loading a case writes nothing, so reads are not accountable.
